title: Epistolae Et Decreta
author: Symmachus
source: Translated by Claude from tmp999.tmp999.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: Dubiam eam fecerunt nostra peccata, æstimantibus quibusdam non posse inter Nestorii et Eutychetis salutis viam mediam reperiri; sed quod omnino necesse sit, aut illius esse quemquam, aut illius. Propter hoc festina post Deum nos adjuvare : et sicut inter Arii dividentis atque separantis unam deitatis naturam atque substantiam, et Sabellii quoque confundentis personas et minuentis numerum trinitatis, ostenderunt sanctissimi Patres viam mediam veritatis, in confessione divinitatis unam substantiam, n auram, virtutemque demonstrantes, propter Sabellium tres personas et æquæ potentiæ unam veritatem : sic et vos nunc, sanctissimi atque beatissimi, illuminate nos spiritualis scientiae vestræ lumine, quae est inter sententiam Eutychelis ad imitationem Sabellii naturas atque substantias confundentis, et inter Nestorii ad imitationem Arii personas atque substantias dividentis, vera rectae fidei confessio, tradita nobis a papa Leone inter sanctos constituto, et discipulorum in Chalcedone sanctorum Patrum duarum substantiarum aut naturarum unitas in una eademque persona et substantia magni Dei et Salvatoris nostri Jesu Chrisli.
passages.english: Our sins have made it doubtful, since some think that no middle way of salvation can be found between Nestorius and Eutyches, but that it is altogether necessary for anyone to belong either to the one or to the other. For this reason hasten, after God, to help us. Just as, between Arius, who divides and separates the one nature and substance of the deity, and Sabellius, who confounds the persons and diminishes the number of the Trinity, the most holy Fathers showed the middle way of truth, setting forth in the confession of the divinity one substance, nature and power, and against Sabellius three persons and one truth of equal power, so you too now, most holy and most blessed ones, enlighten us with the light of your spiritual knowledge [as to] what, between the opinion of Eutyches, who in imitation of Sabellius confounds the natures and substances, and [that] of Nestorius, who in imitation of Arius divides the persons and substances, is the true confession of the right faith, handed down to us by Pope Leo, now placed among the saints, and [the teaching] of the disciples, the holy Fathers at Chalcedon: the unity of two substances or natures in one and the same person and substance of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ.
passages.notes: 'n auram' read as 'naturam'; 'Eutychelis' as 'Eutychetis'; 'Chrisli' as 'Christi'. 'Dubiam eam' refers to something (probably the faith or the way of salvation) named in the preceding, missing text. The construction of 'quae est ... vera rectae fidei confessio' is loose; it is taken as an indirect question. 'et discipulorum ... Patrum' is grammatically unclear; it is read as a second source of the teaching. The phrase 'una eademque persona et substantia' is odd in a Chalcedonian context ('substantia' probably in the sense of hypostasis), but it is translated as written.

passages.original: Ad Augustae majestatis Gratiani imperatoris epistolam octo libris beatus respondit Ambrosius, quia pro fide catholica et illum non piguit prolixius præ.. dicare, et hic non fast divit gratanter accipere. Hæc dixerim, ut si modum libelli promendo collegerim, non existimer quae non oportuit locutus.
passages.english: To the letter of His August Majesty the Emperor Gratian the blessed Ambrose replied in eight books, because for the catholic faith neither was it irksome to him to preach at greater length, nor did this [emperor] disdain to receive [it] gladly. I would say this so that, if I have gathered up the measure of a [short] book in setting [this] forth, I may not be thought to have said what I ought not.
passages.notes: Several scanning errors read as intended: 'præ.. dicare' as 'praedicare', 'fast divit' as 'fastidivit'. 'Collegerim' (rendered 'gathered up') is uncertain. The sense seems to be 'if I have exceeded the measure of a short book', and the text may be corrupt here (perhaps 'excesserim'). 'Eight books' presumably refers to Ambrose's De fide addressed to Gratian, though that work is usually counted as five books.
